fields.meta_title: Membership Landing Page Builder for Clubs | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a membership landing page from a prompt. See four examples: tier signups, guild applications, founding spots, and renewal emails.
fields.h1: Build a Membership Landing Page for Clubs, Guilds, and Studios
fields.hero_description: Get a membership landing page that signs up members by tier and saves each new member to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Your Page Does With Each New Member
fields.features_subheading: One prompt sets up the tiers and the join form, plus the person who hears about each new member.
fields.feature_1:
Describe the membership, get the page

Write your tiers and the join form in plain English, with a price beside each tier, and Emergent builds the page with the table behind it. A new tier later takes one more prompt.
fields.feature_2:
Every member in a table you own

Each signup is saved to a database you own, with the tier and the join date in their own columns next to the contact details. Filter by tier to see which offer brings people in.
fields.feature_3:
Spot limits and end dates

Put a cap on a tier or an end date on an offer in the prompt. The app counts signups against the cap, shows visitors what is left, and changes the page when a limit is reached.
fields.feature_4:
A person hears about each new member

Name who should know when someone joins or applies. Each signup sends that person an email or a Slack message with the member's details, plus any reminders you schedule.
fields.feature_5:
Members that sync to your other tools

Connect Stripe, HubSpot, or any other tool with an API, and each new member can sync to the accounts you already run. Data moves in and out; your own table keeps the first record.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain, and the code when you want it

Put the page on your club's own domain; custom domains are included and use credits. Paid plans add full code export to your GitHub repository, where you can keep building.

fields.tab_content_1:
Full Access is the tier 35 of 64 chose

Foundry Row Makerspace lists its three tiers side by side: Weekend at $45 a month, Full Access at $95, and Studio Desk at $180. This month 64 people joined: 22 Weekend, 35 Full Access, and 7 Studio Desk. Each Studio Desk signup is emailed to shop manager Wendell Okafor, who assigns the desk.
fields.tab_content_2:
Every application waits for Odette Varga

The Lakeshore Bookbinders Guild admits members by application: a portfolio link and the names of 2 current members. The app emails every application to membership chair Odette Varga. Of 14 applications this quarter, she has approved 9 and 5 are waiting. Henrik Solberg's welcome email named the April 12 orientation.
fields.tab_content_3:
When spot 40 is claimed, the price goes to $150

Kilnhouse Ceramics Studio opens with 40 founding memberships at $120 a month, against a standard rate of $150. The join page shows how many founding spots are left: 31 are claimed and 9 remain. When the count reaches 0, the page switches to the $150 rate on its own, with no edit from the studio.
fields.tab_content_4:
Thirty days out, every member gets a renewal link

Each of the 212 Cedar Hollow Garden Club memberships renews on the date the member joined. The app emails a renewal link 30 days before that date, then again 7 days before if the member has not renewed. In November 18 were due: 11 renewed and 7 got the 7-day email.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Membership Landing Page
fields.howto_description: These seven steps build a membership landing page that shows every tier's price, signs people up, and tells the right person.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Say what a member gets in one line
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Show the price of every tier
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Describe it all in one prompt
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write one sentence a stranger could repeat to a friend: what members get and how often they get it. Make it the headline, and put the full list of benefits under it.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Put the price of every tier on the page, next to what that tier adds. A visitor comparing two tiers should never have to open a second page or email you to ask.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Let people join on the spot when anyone can be a member. Ask for an application when someone has to approve each new member, and decide who that person is.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Tell Emergent the tiers, the fields on the join form, and who gets an alert for each signup. Emergent builds the page and the member table together, and a later prompt edits either one.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Set the caps and the renewal dates
fields.howto_step_5_des: Write each limit into the prompt: a cap on founding spots, a close date for an offer, or the day each membership renews. Then say what the page shows once a limit is reached.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Join your own page from a phone
fields.howto_step_6_des: Open the published page on a phone and sign up with your own email. Check that the row reached the member table with the right tier and that the alert reached the right person.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Share it where members already talk
fields.howto_step_7_des: Post the link in your newsletter and in the emails current members already open. Each month, compare signups by tier and rework the tier that drew the fewest.

faq_plan.q: What is a membership landing page?
faq_plan.a: A membership landing page is a single page that sells one membership: what members get, what each tier costs, and a way to join or apply. Point every invitation and flyer at it. A visitor can then decide and join without browsing a whole site.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a membership landing page?
faq_plan.a: Describe the membership to Emergent's AI landing page builder in plain English: the tiers with their prices, and what should happen after someone joins. Emergent builds the page and a member table in a database you own. Publish it, join once yourself to test it, then share the link.

faq_plan.q: What should I look for in membership landing page examples?
faq_plan.a: Look at how each example handles price and proof, not its colors. Note where each tier's price sits, how many fields the join form asks for, and what a visitor sees right after joining. Then copy the structure that matches how people join your group: on the spot, or by application.

faq_plan.q: Should a membership landing page show prices or ask people to get in touch?
faq_plan.a: Show the prices. A visitor choosing between two tiers needs the numbers in front of them, and a get-in-touch button adds a wait before anyone can join. If a price varies, for a student or a household, show the starting price and the rule. The same idea runs through any high converting landing page: one offer and one clear next step.

faq_plan.q: How many tiers should a membership landing page offer?
faq_plan.a: Start with 2 or 3. Each tier should add one thing the tier below it lacks, such as studio access or guest passes. A visitor should be able to see that difference in a single line. If you cannot name it, merge the two tiers into one.

faq_plan.q: Should a membership landing page let people join right away or apply first?
faq_plan.a: Ask people to apply first when membership depends on a vouch or a review, such as a guild that checks portfolios; otherwise let them join right away. Say on the page how long a decision takes and what happens after approval. An applicant then knows when to expect an answer.

faq_plan.q: How do I get current members to share my membership landing page?
faq_plan.a: Give each current member a link to share and a reason to share it, such as a guest pass or a free first month for the friend. Build a referral landing page that records which member sent each signup. Then you can thank or reward the right person. Keep the offer on the page itself, not only in the email.

faq_plan.q: What should the signup form on a membership landing page ask for?
faq_plan.a: Ask only for what you need to admit and reach the member: name, email, and tier. Add a field when someone will act on it, such as a phone number for event reminders or a skill level for class placement. In the app Emergent builds, each answer is saved to its own column in a database you own.

faq_plan.q: Do I need a full membership website or just a membership landing page?
faq_plan.a: Start with a landing page if what you need now is signups: one page with the tiers and a join form. Build a full member site when members need to log in for content or bookings, and keep the landing page as the front door. A later prompt can add the member area to the same app Emergent built.

faq_plan.q: Can a local business sell a yearly plan with a membership landing page?
faq_plan.a: Yes. A yearly plan, such as a car wash club or a repair shop's maintenance plan, sells the same way as a club membership. Show what the member gets each month and the yearly price, then add a join form for the details the shop needs. If the shop sells cars or one-off service appointments instead, an automotive landing page is the better fit.

plan.angle: The results for this keyword are example galleries (LandingPageFlow, Strikingly, Pinterest), membership-platform guides and a Webflow component: they show how a membership page looks and never what happens to a signup once someone joins. This page shows four membership landing pages that a makerspace, a craft guild, a new ceramics studio and a garden club build from a prompt, and follows each signup to where it goes: tier choices counted by tier, applications emailed to the membership chair for a decision, founding spots counted down until the standard rate takes over, and renewal emails sent before each member's renewal date. The FAQ covers the definition, building one, what to take from examples, showing prices, tier count, application versus instant joining, member referrals, form fields, a full membership site versus one page, and car clubs.
